messages.subject: "Factor scores"
parts:
I imagine that I am about to come across as one of these cranks who obsesses about just one thing and goes around insisting that everyone agree with him on that one thing.
     Nevertheless . . .
     So many people are posting about the "factor scores" that lavaan, Mplus, and other packages produce.  (LISREL calls them "latent variable scores.")  Please remember that these are not factor scores at all (Guttman 1955).  Common factors are typically indeterminate, which means that they can only be partly reproduced by a weighted sum of observed variables.  This weighted sum part is what software produces when you ask for factor scores, so they would better be called "determinate factor subscores."  These scores do not behave identically with factors.  In particular, they do not conform to the assumed orthogonality between predictor factors and structural error terms.
     The other part of a true factor score is indeterminate.  Any vector which is orthogonal to all the variables in the model and has the same variance as the factor can be used.  This means that a wide variety of such vectors can be constructed.  The different sets if factor scores that thus result need not be highly correlated with each other, and they need not have similar correlations with variables outside the model.  These vectors are arbitrary but not random--they can be highly correlated with outside variables, or they can be orthogonal with such variables.
     A true factor score is a weighted sum of the determinate part and the indeterminate part.  The weighting depends on the degree of indeterminacy in the model.  The more indicators and the stronger the loadings, the less the indeterminacy, but with just a few indicators, as is usually the case in practice, indeterminacy can be fairly high.
     I know, you can't attach a footnote to everything, and we all use shortcuts in describing familiar things.  But I do worry that there are users who are misled by the name "factor score," who believe that the scores produced by software are in some sense perfectly equivalent to the factors in their models.
--Ed Rigdon

Dear Ed,
I think that your commentary is useful! I had heard of that but a word of caution is always welcome. Looking a bit into that, I have two additional questions:
1/ Concerning the extraction of the factor scores to use then as predictors or outcomes, Muthen said on Mplus forum, : "[factor scores] are biased but when used as independent variables, the bias cancels out so the regression slopes are not biased. » And she also says «  They should be used as . They should not be used as dependent variables in any case. »   I have no idea what the . means in the first part of this sentence. And also, it seems that extracting the scores and trying to use them as dependent variables is a bad idea (which is ennoying as it was my plan!)? Any idea why?
2/ Does the indeterminacy issue also applies to latent growth modeling. After all, intercept and slope can be calculated based on observed data for any participant and do not depend on a weighted sum (or I am wrong?) Also, I have used multilevel mixed models to estimate growth models and it gives the same results without use of latent factors, so that it does not seem that latent variables are really necessary for this model, contrary to a CFA? If the indeterminacy issue does not apply to LGM, can I use I and S as dependent variables?
Thanks a lot!
JB

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: "Factor scores"
parts:
JB--
     I don't know the context in which Linda was commenting, so it's hard for me to evaluate.  You have to say that these pseudo factor scores are biased because they cannot be consistent.  They cannot be consistent because there is no one true factor score value for these pseudo scores to approach.
     It is hard for me to grasp how it would be different to use them as predictors or as dependents.  If the factor (as is usual) is indeterminate, then the indeterminate piece of the true factor score could be chosen to be equal to the part of any variable not included in the original factor model which is orthogonal to the variables in the original model.  Alternatively, as Louis Guttman showed, you could create another set of factor scores where the indeterminate piece is -1 times that same component.  Or the indeterminate part could be "white noise," but that's not necessary.  All three sets of scores could be equally appropriate sets of factor scores for the same factor.  So different choices for this indeterminate component would have consequences for your results, whether the factor scores are in the role of predictor or dependent.
     Regarding latent growth modeling, the answer depends on whether the same rank problem arises in growth models that arises in conventional factor models.  At root, factor indeterminacy is a rank problem.  In a conventional factor analysis, you have p observed variables, so the rank of the observed covariance matrix is p.  On the other side, you have p specific factors (error terms) plus the common factor, which are all presumed independent of each other.  So when you try to turn the p dimensions of information in the data into p + 1 dimensions of information, you get indeterminacy.
     If you have the same assumption of independence in a latent growth model, then you have the same indeterminacy problem.  In a typical latent growth model, you impose constraints on the error term variances, but I think you are still dealing with p error terms, plus, say, the intercept and slope factors.  So I would expect that you face the same problem.  I would be happy to be proven wrong.
--Ed Rigdon
